units.text:
Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) • Page 2

1. Introduction to ODEs

An ordinary differential equation is an equation involving an unknown function of one independent variable and one or more of its derivatives. ODEs are used to describe quantities that change with respect to another variable, such as time, distance or position.

Basic terminology

• The order of an ODE is the highest derivative appearing in the equation.

• The degree is the power of the highest-order derivative after the equation has been made polynomial in its

derivatives.

• An ODE is linear if the dependent variable and its derivatives occur only to the first power and are not

multiplied together.

• A solution is a function that satisfies the differential equation on an appropriate interval.

Example 1 — Identify order and degree

• Consider: y''' + 4y'' - y' + 7y = 0.

• The highest derivative is y''', so the order is 3. The highest derivative occurs to the first power, so the

degree is 1.

Example 2 — Classify an ODE

• Consider: y' + 3y = x².

• This is a first-order linear ODE because y and y' occur only to the first power and are not multiplied

together.

Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) • Page 3

2. First-Order ODEs: Separation of Variables

A separable differential equation can be rearranged so that all terms involving the dependent variable are on one side and all terms involving the independent variable are on the other.

General pattern

• If dy/dx = f(x)g(y), rearrange to dy/g(y) = f(x) dx, then integrate both sides.

Example 3 — Separable equation

• Solve dy/dx = 3x²y.

• Separate: dy/y = 3x² dx.

• Integrate: ln|y| = x³ + C.

• Therefore: y = Ce^(x³).

Example 4 — Separable equation with an initial condition

• Solve dy/dx = 2xy, given y(0) = 5.

• Separate: dy/y = 2x dx.

• Integrate: ln|y| = x² + C, so y = Ce^(x²).

• Using y(0)=5 gives C=5.

• Therefore: y = 5e^(x²).

Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) • Page 4

3. First-Order Linear ODEs

A first-order linear ODE can be written in the standard form dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x). It is commonly solved using an integrating factor.

Integrating factor

• The integrating factor is μ(x) = e^(∫P(x)dx). Multiplying the equation by μ converts the left-hand side into the

derivative of μy.

Example 5 — Integrating factor method

• Solve dy/dx + 2y = 4.

• Here P(x)=2, so μ=e^(∫2dx)=e^(2x).

• Multiply through: e^(2x)y' + 2e^(2x)y = 4e^(2x).

• Thus d/dx(e^(2x)y)=4e^(2x).

• Integrating gives e^(2x)y=2e^(2x)+C.

• Therefore: y=2+Ce^(-2x).

Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) • Page 5

4. Applications and Initial-Value Problems

An initial-value problem gives a differential equation together with a condition such as y(xn)=yn. The condition determines the arbitrary constant in the general solution.

Example 6 — Initial-value problem

• Solve y' = 6x - 4, given y(1)=3.

• Integrate: y = 3x² - 4x + C.

• Apply y(1)=3: 3 - 4 + C = 3, so C=4.

• Therefore: y = 3x² - 4x + 4.

Common interpretation

• An ODE may describe a rate of change. For example, if y represents the amount of a quantity at time t,

then dy/dt represents its instantaneous rate of change. An initial condition specifies the starting state.

Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) • Page 6

5. Second-Order Linear ODEs

A common second-order linear homogeneous ODE has the form ay'' + by' + cy = 0, where a, b and c are constants. We use the characteristic equation to determine the form of the solution.

Characteristic equation

• Assume y=e^(rx). Substitution gives the characteristic equation ar²+br+c=0.

• If the roots are distinct real numbers rn and rn, then y=Cne^(rnx)+Cne^(rnx).

• If there is a repeated root r, then y=(Cn+Cnx)e^(rx).

Example 7 — Distinct roots

• Solve y'' - 5y' + 6y = 0.

• Characteristic equation: r² - 5r + 6 = 0.

• Factor: (r-2)(r-3)=0, giving r=2 and r=3.

• Therefore: y=Cne^(2x)+Cne^(3x).

Find the integrating factor: The integrating factor is μ(x) = e^(∫P(x)dx).
Multiply the equation by μ: This converts the left-hand side into the derivative of μy.
Integrate both sides: Solve for y by integrating the resulting equation.

Apply the initial condition: Substitute the given values into the general solution to determine C.
Write the particular solution: Replace C with the value found in the previous step.

sections.title: Second-Order Linear ODEs: Characteristic Equation
paragraphs: A common second-order linear homogeneous ODE has the form ay'' + by' + cy = 0, where a, b and c are constants. We use the characteristic equation to determine the form of the solution. The nature of the roots of the characteristic equation dictates the structure of the general solution.

evidence.quote:
Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) • Page 6

5. Second-Order Linear ODEs

A common second-order linear homogeneous ODE has the form ay'' + by' + cy = 0, where a, b and c are constants. We use the characteristic equation to determine the form of the solution.

Characteristic equation

• Assume y=e^(rx). Substitution gives the characteristic equation ar²+br+c=0.

• If the roots are distinct real numbers rn and rn, then y=Cne^(rnx)+Cne^(rnx).

• If there is a repeated root r, then y=(Cn+Cnx)e^(rx).

Example 7 — Distinct roots

• Solve y'' - 5y' + 6y = 0.

• Characteristic equation: r² - 5r + 6 = 0.

• Factor: (r-2)(r-3)=0, giving r=2 and r=3.

• Therefore: y=Cne^(2x)+Cne^(3x).

steps: Assume a solution of the form y=e^(rx).
Substitute into the ODE to obtain the characteristic equation ar²+br+c=0.
Solve the characteristic equation for r.
If the roots are distinct real numbers r₁ and r₂, then the general solution is y=C₁e^(r₁x)+C₂e^(r₂x).
If there is a repeated root r, then the general solution is y=(C₁+C₂x)e^(rx).
Example 7: To solve y'' - 5y' + 6y = 0, form the characteristic equation r² - 5r + 6 = 0, factor to (r-2)(r-3)=0 giving r=2 and r=3, and conclude y=C₁e^(2x)+C₂e^(3x).

units.text:
LAN, WAN and MAN • Page 2

1. Introduction to Computer Networks

A computer network is a collection of interconnected devices that communicate and share resources. Devices can include computers, servers, printers, phones, switches, routers and wireless access points.

Why networks matter

• Resource sharing: files, printers, applications and internet connections can be shared.

• Communication: users and systems can exchange information.

• Centralized services: organizations can provide shared storage, authentication and applications.

• Scalability: additional devices and locations can be connected as requirements grow.

Geographical classification

• One useful classification is geographical scope. LAN generally covers a small area, MAN a metropolitan

area, and WAN a large geographical area such as a region, country or continent.

LAN, WAN and MAN • Page 4

3. LAN Components and Technologies

A LAN uses networking devices and transmission technologies to connect local devices.

Common components

• Switch: connects devices on an Ethernet LAN and forwards frames toward their destinations.

• Wireless access point: provides Wi-Fi connectivity.

• Router: connects the LAN to other networks.

• Network interface: provides wired or wireless network connectivity to a device.

• Ethernet cabling: commonly provides wired LAN connections.

LAN topology

• Modern Ethernet LANs commonly use a star arrangement in which devices connect to a central switch.

Wireless LANs commonly use access points as central connection points.

LAN, WAN and MAN • Page 5

4. Metropolitan Area Network (MAN)

A Metropolitan Area Network connects networks across a metropolitan or city-scale area. It is larger than a typical LAN but generally smaller than a WAN.

Characteristics

• City or metropolitan-scale coverage.

• Can connect multiple LANs.

• May use high-capacity fiber-optic links.

• Requires more extensive infrastructure than a single-site LAN.

• May be operated by an organization, service provider or partnership.

Examples

• A university connecting campuses across one city.

• A government organization connecting offices throughout a metropolitan area.

• A provider's metropolitan network linking customers and facilities.

LAN, WAN and MAN • Page 8

7. WAN Devices, Services and Technologies

WAN connectivity requires systems capable of moving traffic between geographically separated networks. Routers are central because they make forwarding decisions between networks.

Common components

• Routers: forward packets between different networks.

• WAN links: communication paths connecting distant sites.

• Provider services: telecommunications providers may supply connectivity between locations.

• Firewalls and security gateways: help control traffic entering and leaving networks.

WAN approaches

• Organizations may use dedicated connectivity, provider-managed services, internet-based connections,

or combinations. The choice depends on cost, reliability, performance and security requirements.

LAN, WAN and MAN • Page 10

9. How LAN, MAN and WAN Work Together

These categories are not isolated. A large organization can use LANs at individual sites, metropolitan connectivity between nearby sites, and WAN connectivity between distant regions.

Example

• A university can have a LAN in each faculty building.

• A metropolitan connection can link campuses around the same city.

• A WAN can connect those campuses to a remote campus or cloud infrastructure.

• Routers connect separate networks while switches and access points provide local connectivity.

Key idea

• LAN, MAN and WAN describe different networking scales. A network can therefore be part of a larger

interconnected system.

1. Introduction to Computer Networks

A computer network is a collection of interconnected devices that communicate and share resources. Devices can include computers, servers, printers, phones, switches, routers and wireless access points.

Why networks matter

• Resource sharing: files, printers, applications and internet connections can be shared.

• Communication: users and systems can exchange information.

• Centralized services: organizations can provide shared storage, authentication and applications.

• Scalability: additional devices and locations can be connected as requirements grow.

Geographical classification

• One useful classification is geographical scope. LAN generally covers a small area, MAN a metropolitan

area, and WAN a large geographical area such as a region, country or continent.

3. LAN Components and Technologies

A LAN uses networking devices and transmission technologies to connect local devices.

Common components

• Switch: connects devices on an Ethernet LAN and forwards frames toward their destinations.

• Wireless access point: provides Wi-Fi connectivity.

• Router: connects the LAN to other networks.

• Network interface: provides wired or wireless network connectivity to a device.

• Ethernet cabling: commonly provides wired LAN connections.

LAN topology

• Modern Ethernet LANs commonly use a star arrangement in which devices connect to a central switch.

Wireless LANs commonly use access points as central connection points.

questions.prompt: What type of network connects networks across a metropolitan or city-scale area?

4. Metropolitan Area Network (MAN)

A Metropolitan Area Network connects networks across a metropolitan or city-scale area. It is larger than a typical LAN but generally smaller than a WAN.

Characteristics

• City or metropolitan-scale coverage.

• Can connect multiple LANs.

• May use high-capacity fiber-optic links.

• Requires more extensive infrastructure than a single-site LAN.

• May be operated by an organization, service provider or partnership.

Examples

• A university connecting campuses across one city.

• A government organization connecting offices throughout a metropolitan area.

• A provider's metropolitan network linking customers and facilities.

7. WAN Devices, Services and Technologies

WAN connectivity requires systems capable of moving traffic between geographically separated networks. Routers are central because they make forwarding decisions between networks.

Common components

• Routers: forward packets between different networks.

• WAN links: communication paths connecting distant sites.

• Provider services: telecommunications providers may supply connectivity between locations.

• Firewalls and security gateways: help control traffic entering and leaving networks.

WAN approaches

• Organizations may use dedicated connectivity, provider-managed services, internet-based connections,

or combinations. The choice depends on cost, reliability, performance and security requirements.

questions.prompt: How can a large organization use LANs, MANs and WANs together?
questions.answerQuote: A large organization can use LANs at individual sites, metropolitan connectivity between nearby sites, and WAN connectivity between distant regions.

evidence.quote:
LAN, WAN and MAN • Page 10

9. How LAN, MAN and WAN Work Together

These categories are not isolated. A large organization can use LANs at individual sites, metropolitan connectivity between nearby sites, and WAN connectivity between distant regions.

Example

• A university can have a LAN in each faculty building.

• A metropolitan connection can link campuses around the same city.

• A WAN can connect those campuses to a remote campus or cloud infrastructure.

• Routers connect separate networks while switches and access points provide local connectivity.

Key idea

• LAN, MAN and WAN describe different networking scales. A network can therefore be part of a larger

interconnected system.

units.text: Colonialism in Africa refers to the period when European powers took political, economic, and military control over much of the continent, especially from the late 19th century. A major turning point was the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, where European countries divided African territories among themselves with little regard for existing ethnic groups, kingdoms, or boundaries. Colonial governments introduced new legal systems, schools, roads, railways, and administrative structures. However, these developments mainly served colonial interests. African land, labor, minerals, and agricultural resources were heavily exploited, while many local industries and political institutions were weakened. Colonial rule also created artificial borders that later contributed to political and ethnic tensions. From the mid 20th century, African nationalist movements grew stronger, and many countries gained independence during the 1950s and 1960s. The legacy of colonialism remains important today, influencing Africa's borders, languages, economies, and political systems.
